docs.text: Instructions for researchers wanting access to COSMOS-SENS at LUNARC. In order to keep the system orderly we have set out some guidelines which everyone should follow to maintain a smoothly running platform. Please read this document carefully before you use the system. What is COSMOS-SENS? The GDPR is an EU directive that protects the personal information and data of individuals, therefore any identifying data from living subjects has to be kept securely under these rules. COSMOS-SENS is a isolated HPC platform housed at LUNARC where we handle and analyse data of a sensitive nature under GDPR rules. This also covers data which is sensitive for national security. This means COSMOS-SENS does not have a connection to the internet , and transferring data to/from COSMOS-SENS is done via sftp (more later). Who is COSMOS-SENS for? Before requesting an account, you should be comfortable using a LINUX based high-performance computing (HPC) platform. Note COSMOS-SENS is not for general purpose file storage. It is for data being actively worked on. for general storage please contact the RDO. Nodes COSMOS-SENS has a mix of nodes available. They are: 1) 32 x standard nodes . 2 x AMD, 48 cores, 256GB RAM, 2TB temporary directory given by $SNIC_TMP or $TMPDIR . 2) 9 x HiRAM nodes . 2 x AMD, 48 cores, 2TB RAM, 2TB temporary directory given by $SNIC_TMP or $TMPDIR . If you want to send a job to these nodes you need to add #SBATCH -p sens-xl to the preamble of your sbatch script (explained below). -p specifies which partition the job is sent to. 3) 3 x GPU nodes (NVIDIA A40), 2 x 24 cores. 2TB RAM To send jobs here, use #SBATCH -p sens-gpu . Note By default jobs are sent to the standard nodes, so -p does not need to be specified. Make sure your jobs actually need the xl and gpu nodes if you send them there. Getting access to COSMOS-SENS 1) Make an account at SUPR and request a COSMOS-SENS project The PI needs to do the following. First, make an account at SUPR . Be sure to provide a correct mobile phone number since your phone will be needed in the future for two-factor authentication. When in SUPR, apply for a COSMOS-SENS project. [Rounds -> Special Rounds -> Rounds at LUNARC -> COSMOS-SENS]. Apply for a storage project too if you will be working on a large volume of data. When your project is approved you will have the ability to add co-workers to your project. Each of your co-workers will need to make an account on SUPR before they can be added . All are required to do the following after making SUPR accounts: 2) Log back in to SUPR and apply for an account at LUNARC. Left menu under "Accounts". Fill out the details correctly and use your mobile number. This will be needed for 2-factor authentication. 3) Request a Static IP address ( This is important, do this straight after step 2 ) As a further layer of security we employ IP address filtering to make sure only authorised users can establish a connection to COSMOS-SENS. While your LUNARC account is being created, contact LDC (servicedesk@lu.se) and request a VPN with a static IP address. When you receive your IP address, ask the project leader to raise a support ticket (support@lunarc.lu.se) with LUNARC stating what the IP address is, and who it is for. If you use a workstation connected by a cable, ask LDC to fix the IP address for your port number. Communicate this IP address to LUNARC the same way . 4) Sign the agreement LUNARC will send you a digital agreement that you will need sign via EduSign . Both you and the project leader will need to do this. Someone from LUNARC will contact you with details on how you create your password. 5) Setup 2FA LUNARC uses two-factor authentication using Pocket Pass on your smartphone. Follow the instructions here to set this up. 6) Setup the VPN on your laptop/workstation Go to the LDC guide here and setup the VPN on your device. When you click on the link it will look like a blank page. You need to login using Lucat (top-right) to see all connection options . WARNING DO NOT SHARE YOUR PASSWORD! This volates the terms of the agreement and your account will be disabled. Connecting to COSMOS-SENS Note Do not forget to activate your static VPN before you try to connect The only way to interface with COSMOS-SENS is via a Linux desktop. Point your browser to: https://sensXX.lunarc.lu.se where XX will be the group number supplied to you by LUNARC. Login with your LUNARC credentials (not Lucat) using two-factor authentication via Pocket Pass. You will be presented with the option of two GNOME desktops you can use. Pick the one you prefer. Getting data to COSMOS-SENS Getting data to COSMOS-SENS can only be done via sftp via the diode ( cs-diode.lunarc.lu.se ). This can made easier by mounting a COSMOS-SENS folder to folder on the local machine you are working on. Files can then be copied/moved to this mounted folder which will then become available on COSMOS-SENS. You will need to install sshfs if you haven't already. For Linux machines the sshfs package can be installed via your package manager, and for Mac users there is FUSE-T . Windows users will have to transfer files using WinSCP with the 2FA option or Filezilla with the interactive login option. To mount a folder (Linux/macOS) do the following: 1) Login to COSMOS-SENS and make a folder. For example mkdir FileTransferFolder 2) Make a folder on your local machine that you will mount to. For example ToCSENS 3) To mount the folder on COSMOS-SENS to your local machine do: sshfs <userID>@cs-diode.lunarc.lu.se:/<pathto>/FileTransferFolder/ ToCSENS/ So if your FileTransferFolder was made in /home (on COSMOS) it would look something like: sshfs <userid>@cs-diode.lunarc.lu.se:/home/<userid>/FileTransferFolder/ ToCSENS/ 4) You can now copy/move files into ToCSENS on your local machine where they will be available in COSMOS-SENS. Equally, copying/moving files into FileTransferFolder on COSMOS-SENS will make them available on your local computer. 5) When you are done with the connection to COSMOS-SENS, you can unmount the folder by doing umount ToCSENS To be clear, all files in this mounted folder are located on COSMOS-SENS . When you unmount ToCSENS that folder will be empty again. Be smart The point of COSMOS-SENS is to protect sensitive data, so be mindful about which folders you mount locally. For example, mounting /home/<user> would expose everything you have in your home folder to your local machine. If a bad actor were to try something malicious on your local computer, they would also have access to everything you have on COSMOS-SENS. Also, everything in your /home would also be exposed to any mistakes you make on you local machine. Mount specific folders rather than absolutely everything. Better safe than sorry. Cut & Paste Let's get this out of the way now. Cut and paste is not allowed from COSMOS-SENS outwards, i.e you cannot ctrl-c in COSMOS and ctrl-v to a window on your local machine. You can paste into COSMOS using the clipboard which is located on the left side of the screen. Click on the arrow to pull it out. The easiest way to C&P is to mount a COSMOS-SENS folder on to your local machine, and then just have a simple text file open in this window that can be open on both COSMOS and your local computer. This can then be a two-way clipboard between the two systems. Where do I put my data? There are two main folders on COSMOS-SENS: After logging in you will land in your home folder ( /home/<userid> ). You will also have another folder called /scale/grXX/shared/ where all members of your group can put files to share. Files cannot be shared between groups, i.e, members of gr01 cannot send files to people in gr02. The two front-ends cannot touch. Is my data backed up? No Data on COSMOS-SENS does not have a backup. It is important you are comfortable in Linux environment, and so are individuals you add oto the project. Modules Software at LUNARC is organised into modules which are loaded when needed, usually when a job is submitted. a rundown of the module system can be seen here , but lets load bowtie2 as an example: First we find the options available using module spider : $ module spider bowtie2 ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- Bowtie2: ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- Description: Bowtie 2 is an ultrafast and memory-efficient tool for aligning sequencing reads to long reference sequences. It is particularly good at aligning reads of about 50 up to 100s or 1,000s of characters, and particularly good at aligning to relatively long (e.g. mammalian) genomes. Bowtie 2 indexes the genome with an FM Index to keep its memory footprint small: for the human genome, its memory footprint is typically around 3.2 GB. Bowtie 2 supports gapped, local, and paired-end alignment modes. Versions: Bowtie2/2.2.6 Bowtie2/2.2.8 Bowtie2/2.2.9 Bowtie2/2.3.2 Bowtie2/2.3.4.1 Bowtie2/2.3.4.2 Bowtie2/2.4.4 ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- For detailed information about a specific "Bowtie2" module (including how to load the modules) use the module's full name. For example: $ module spider Bowtie2/2.3.4.1 ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- You can see there are several version available. To see how to load version 2.4.4 we need to run `module spider again: $ module spider Bowtie2/2.4.4 ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- Bowtie2: Bowtie2/2.4.4 ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- Description: Bowtie 2 is an ultrafast and memory-efficient tool for aligning sequencing reads to long reference sequences. It is particularly good at aligning reads of about 50 up to 100s or 1,000s of characters, and particularly good at aligning to relatively long (e.g. mammalian) genomes. Bowtie 2 indexes the genome with an FM Index to keep its memory footprint small: for the human genome, its memory footprint is typically around 3.2 GB. Bowtie 2 supports gapped, local, and paired-end alignment modes. You will need to load all module(s) on any one of the lines below before the "Bowtie2/2.4.4" module is available to load. GCC/10.3.0 So to load bowtie2, we also need to load the GCC/10.3.0 module. So we can now load bowtie2 by doing: $ module load GCC/10.3.0 Bowtie2/2.4.4 A short way of doing this is: $ ml GCC/10.3.0 Bowtie2/2.4.4 Done. If you have too many module conflicts happening, you can wipe the slate clean with: $ module purge Installing software For software installation requests, raise a support ticket with LUNARC providing a link to the software that needs to be installed. Running jobs When you login into COSMOS-SENS you will be located on the front-end (FE). THE FE is not a place to run long computations , only small interactive jobs. Long memory and processor intensive jobs must be sent to a compute node. SLURM Any jobs such as making and mapping fastq files should be sent to the blades, and for this, LUNARC uses the SLURM job submission system. See below and here for basic guidelines on how to submit a job. Project code Your project will have a project ID associated with it (csens20XX-X-X format). You need this to run a job. Lets say you want to map reads using bowtie, an example header for a job Run_bowtie.sh could look like this: #! /bin/bash #SBATCH -n 5 #SBATCH -N 1 #SBATCH -t 24:00:00 #SBATCH -A csens20XX-X-X #SBATCH -J BT2 #SBATCH -o BT2.%j.out #SBATCH -e BT2SingSing.%j.err module purge module load GCC/10.3.0 Bowtie2/2.4.4 bowtie2 <rest of the command here> In short -n 5 requests 5 CPU cores, -N 1 requests one node (do not ask for more), -t 24:00:00 kills the job after 24 hours, -A csens2024-3-2 specifies the project code, -J BT2 is the name of your job, -o BT2.%j.out is the outfile of the job (name+job id), -e BT2.%j.err is where the error log goes. The script is then run using: $ sbatch Run_bowtie.sh You can see your own jobs lining up using: $ sacct All jobs using: $ squeue If you know you have screwed something up and you want to kill a job: $ scancel <jobid> GPU nodes If your program can use GPUs then you can run on the GPU nodes. You will need to add a partition parameter in your SLURM script so: #SBATCH -p sens-gpu Do not forget to load the CUDA modules if you need them: module load CUDA/12.1.1 There are fewer GPU nodes so the queue can be long for these. Run jobs using the local disk! Most jobs create temporary files when running, so it makes sense (where possible) to use the local disk on each compute node to improve speed and reduce network traffic between the node and the storage. SLURM is set up to give you a temporary folder on the nodes for each job you start. The name of your temporary folder is stored in the $SNIC_TMP variable. This variable does not exist on the frontend, and the folder on the node is private to you and will be deleted once the job is finished. So in the last step of your script you need to save your results. For example, your script could look something like: STAR ...\\ --readFilesIn /somewhere/clusterPipeline/merged_cluster/*.gz \\ ... <rest of STAR command>\\ --outFileNamePrefix $SNIC_TMP/out/MyAnalysis_ cp $SNIC_TMP/out/MyAnalysis_* /home/<userid>/pathtofinaldestination/ So in this case, the output is directed to the local disk at $SNIC_TMP/out/MyAnalysis_ , and once mapping is complete the results are copied from there to your main storage in home . Be nice to fellow co-workers Compute resources are sometimes limited, therefore try to use only the resources as you actually need for your jobs. Make sure you read the documents of the software you are using, and whether it can actually handle multi-core processes. There is no point in asking for 10 cores if your software cannot handle it. Reproducible research Never update packages in the middle of a project! . There is always a chance underlying methods change that may cause a change in the results. The best thing you can do is "freeze" your packages buy putting everything into a Apptainer (new name for Singularity) container/environment that you can use knowing that all package version are the same. Apptainer containers are also great for getting software onto COSMOS-SENS without needing LUNARC support to do an install. You can read more about Apptainer images here . Apptainer is installed on COSMOS-SENS and no modules are needed to load it. Apptainer images are very useful for packaging together workflows that require several programs to run one after another. Post-publication, these images can be included in the supporting material of your paper so others in your community can download it and apply it on their own data. COSMOS-SENS and bioinformatics The majority of users on COSMOS-SENS are bioinformaticians processing human sequence data. There are tools that people would like to use in a secure setting, so we will go through a few here. nf-core Note: this document has been updated to show how to run pipelines using Nexflow v24 . The previous document gave instructions for v23. Nextflow and the nf-core pipelines are a fantastic resource for bioinformaticians. There are a multitude of workflows for various NGS applications which go into real depth regarding QC, mapping methods, annotation, and reporting. After a pipeline is run, you also get the version numbers of the software used for easy reporting in papers, but importantly, the pipeline remains the same every time you run it ensuring results are comparable. When an nf-core pipeline is initiated, singularity images are pulled at runtime over the internet for each component program. As COSMOS-SENS is a secure server with no internet connection, pipelines and images have to be downloaded and then transferred to COSMOS-SENS beforehand. Getting an nf-core pipeline Read the nf-core docs, but to download a pipeline you need to install nf-core and then use nf-core tools download to begin the process of downloading a pipeline. You will need to download the singularity images when the option comes up. To make the pipelines available for all your project members, a good place to put them would be the shared area, for example /scale/grXX/shared/nf-core/ . When you download pipelines, make a folder called singularity_cache where the images are downloaded to. Use "copy" when the choice of "copy/amend" comes up during download process. Setting up to use nf-core To use them, you need to add a few lines into a file called .bash_profile which is in your home folder. 1) Open the file using gedit ~/.bash_profile 2) Add these lines at the end, and then save the file: export NXF_OFFLINE='true' export SINGULARITY_TMPDIR=$SNIC_TMP export NXF_SINGULARITY_LIBRARYDIR=/scale/grXX/shared/nf-core/singularity_cache export NXF_SINGULARITY_CACHEDIR="$NXF_SINGULARITY_LIBRARYDIR" export SINGULARITY_CACHEDIR="$NXF_SINGULARITY_LIBRARYDIR" export NXF_HOME=/scale/grXX/shared/nf-core/nextflow_sub/ export NXF_SINGULARITY_HOME_MOUNT=true Make sure you change the paths/name according to your project. You should then logout of COSMOS-SENS and log back in so these changes take effect . These lines set the environment variables that 1) Tells Nextflow where the singularity images are located ( /scale/gr01/shared/nf-core/singularity_cache ) 2) Set the temp dir to the ones located on the nodes ( $SNIC_TMP ). 3) Binds the singularity images to /scale so they can be found system wide. 4) Sets the home of Nextflow to the central copy on shared ( /scale/grXX/shared/nf-core/nextflow_sub/ ). This means each user doesn't need their own. When running a job, use the config file located here: /scale/gr01/shared/nf-core/cosmo_sens_grp1_NFv24.config This file contains the project ID and automatically sets the RAM and core resources so you don't have to. An example using RNAseq A sample sheet ( samplesheet.csv ) would look something like: sample,fastq_1,fastq_2,strandedness Sample1,Sample1_R1.fastq.gz,Sample1_R2.fastq.gz,auto Sample2,Sample2_R1.fastq.gz,Sample2_R2.fastq.gz,auto Sample3,Sample3_R1.fastq.gz,Sample3_R2.fastq.gz,auto and a script NFC_RNAseq.sh running the basic rnaseq pipline would look like this: module load Nextflow/24.10.0 nextflow run /scale/grXX/shared/nf-core/nf-core-rnaseq_3.17.0/3_17_0/main.nf \ -profile singularity \ --input samplesheet.csv \ -c /scale/grXX/shared/nf-core/cosmos_sens_grp1_NFv24.config \ --genome GRCm38 \ --igenomes_base /scale/references/AWS-iGenomes/ \ --outdir /home/<userid>/RNAseq_project/NFC_out This script, the fastq files, and the samplesheet are all in the same folder. The pipline is launched using: sh NFC_RNAseq.sh Cut&Run module load Nextflow/24.10.0 nextflow run /scale/gr01/shared/nf-core/nf-core-cutandrun_3.2.2/3_2_2/main.nf \ --input samplesheet.csv \ -profile singularity \ -c /scale/gr01/shared/nf-core/cosmos_sens_grp1_NFv24.config \ --fasta /scale/references/AWS-iGenomes/Homo_sapiens/Ensembl/GRCh37/Sequence/WholeGenomeFasta/genome.fa \ --gtf /scale/references/AWS-iGenomes/Homo_sapiens/Ensembl/GRCh37/Annotation/Genes \ --spikein_bowtie2 /scale/references/AWS-iGenomes/Escherichia_coli_K_12_MG1655/NCBI/2001-10-15/Sequence/Bowtie2Index \ --spikein_fasta /scale/references/AWS-iGenomes/Escherichia_coli_K_12_MG1655/NCBI/2001-10-15/Sequence/WholeGenomeFasta/genome.fa \ --outdir /home/<userid>/<path_to_out>/CaR_Out Sample sheets The contents of the sample sheet will vary depending on which pipline you are using, so be sure to read the manual. Remove the work folder nf-core pipelines will make a work folder if the tmp folder on the node isn't used. Delete this folder when you are done! It is normally huge and contains nothing of interest. Available pipelines The available pipelines are located in /scale/gr01/shared/nf-core . If the one you need is missing, contact Petter for it to be downloaded. If you have many small fastq files Some well-based methods generate thousands of small fastq files which do not play nice with the queuing system on CSENS when using an nf-core pipeline. The jobs are fired-off to the nodes so quickly that SLURM cannot keep up, but importantly, setting up the task actually takes longer than the compute subsequently done. If you are in this situation, you need to run the pipeline locally on a single node instead. This means all the pipeline steps will be carried out on single server, and not distributed over multiple nodes which is what normally happens. Do this this you have to used a different config file, namely cosmos_sens_grp1_NFv24_local.config . So, to use RNAseq as an example you would submit a job like so: #! /bin/bash #SBATCH -n 48 #SBATCH -N 1 #SBATCH -t 24:00:00 #SBATCH -A csens2024-3-2 #SBATCH -J nfc_rnaseq #SBATCH -o nfc_rnaseq.%j.out #SBATCH -e nfc_rnaseq.%j.err module load Nextflow/24.10.0 nextflow run /scale/gr01/shared/nf-core/nf-core-rnaseq_3.17.0/3_17_0/main.nf \ -profile singularity \ --input samplesheet.csv \ -c /scale/gr01/shared/nf-core/cosmos_sens_grp1_NFv24_local.config \ --genome GRCm38 \ --igenomes_base /references/AWS-iGenomes/ \ --outdir /home/<userid>/RNAseq_project/NFC_out This will run the entire pipeline on a single node. Apptainer (Singularity) containers Software can be packaged into Apptainer containers that provide a complete analysis environment that can be copied over to COSMOS-SENS and be used there. This means you get exactly what you need, and also reduces the workload on the good people at LUNARC. This is also an excellent way of practicing reproducible research . A project can be done using an immutable Apptainer image, so if you need to go back to the project in X years time, you have the original software setup you had when you first did it. If you upgrade a piece of software in your image, you can make a new version of it so the previous version still exists in the original state. It's easier to make an image on a Linux system if you are going to use it on COSMOS-SENS. If you use a Mac, your best bet is to use open COSMOS to make the image which you can copy to COSMOS-SENS. We have a tutorial which Stefan Lang has written showing how to make images on COSMOS that you can read here . If you are making an image on your own Linux machine , an example is given below. Minimal example (taken from Stefan's tutorial ). This is an Apptainer definition file for creating a container based on Alpine Linux with Python, JupyterLab, R, and R-Jupyter integration. We use Alpine Linux for this because it produces slim images that take up less space. Put the following into a file called Apptainer_example.def : Bootstrap: docker From: alpine:latest # Use the latest Alpine Linux image as the base %post # Update the package index and install essential packages apk update # Install build tools and libraries required for Python and R # You must not have comments after the '\' in the following lines! apk add --no-cache bash \ build-base \ zeromq-dev \ libffi-dev \ musl-dev \ openblas-dev \ R \ R-dev \ R-doc \ python3 \ py3-pip \ python3-dev \ py3-setuptools \ py3-wheel # Allow pip to modify system-wide packages (ChatGPT forgets that ALWAYS) export PIP_BREAK_SYSTEM_PACKAGES=1 # Install JupyterLab using pip pip3 install --no-cache-dir jupyterlab # Install R packages for Jupyter integration R -e "install.packages(c('IRkernel', 'IRdisplay'), repos='https://cloud.r-project.org/')" # Set up IRkernel to make R available as a Jupyter kernel R -e "IRkernel::installspec(user = FALSE)" %environment # Ensure /usr/local/bin is in the PATH so JupyterLab can be found export PATH="/usr/local/bin:$PATH" # if you want to install more python packages in the sandbox: export PIP_BREAK_SYSTEM_PACKAGES=1 %runscript # By default, run JupyterLab when the container starts jupyter lab --port 9734 --ip=0.0.0.0 --allow-root --no-browser To build a sandbox for manual modification, run this command: apptainer build --sandbox Apptainer_example Apptainer_example.def Shell into the sandbox: apptainer shell --writable Apptainer_example From here you can now install anything else you might need using Alpine's apk add --no-cache command. After you have installed everything, including the jupyter lab server, you can test it with: apptainer run Apptainer_example If you're happy, you can then go ahead and build the image: apptainer build Apptainer_example.sif Apptainer_example The image can now be copied to COSMOS-SENS and used there using: apptainer run Apptainer_example.sif Again, if you are making an image on COSMOS you need to read Stefan's tutorial .

Windows users will have to transfer files using WinSCP with the 2FA option or Filezilla with the interactive login option. To mount a folder (Linux/macOS) do the following: 1) Login to COSMOS-SENS and make a folder. For example mkdir FileTransferFolder 2) Make a folder on your local machine that you will mount to. For example ToCSENS 3) To mount the folder on COSMOS-SENS to your local machine do: sshfs <userID>@cs-diode.lunarc.lu.se:/<pathto>/FileTransferFolder/ ToCSENS/ So if your FileTransferFolder was made in /home (on COSMOS) it would look something like: sshfs <userid>@cs-diode.lunarc.lu.se:/home/<userid>/FileTransferFolder/ ToCSENS/ 4) You can now copy/move files into ToCSENS on your local machine where they will be available in COSMOS-SENS. Equally, copying/moving files into FileTransferFolder on COSMOS-SENS will make them available on your local computer. 5) When you are done with the connection to COSMOS-SENS, you can unmount the folder by doing umount ToCSENS To be clear, all files in this mounted folder are located on COSMOS-SENS . When you unmount ToCSENS that folder will be empty again. Be smart The point of COSMOS-SENS is to protect sensitive data, so be mindful about which folders you mount locally. For example, mounting /home/<user> would expose everything you have in your home folder to your local machine. If a bad actor were to try something malicious on your local computer, they would also have access to everything you have on COSMOS-SENS. Also, everything in your /home would also be exposed to any mistakes you make on you local machine. Mount specific folders rather than absolutely everything. Better safe than sorry.
docs.title: Getting data to COSMOS-SENS

docs.text: Let's get this out of the way now. Cut and paste is not allowed from COSMOS-SENS outwards, i.e you cannot ctrl-c in COSMOS and ctrl-v to a window on your local machine. You can paste into COSMOS using the clipboard which is located on the left side of the screen. Click on the arrow to pull it out. The easiest way to C&P is to mount a COSMOS-SENS folder on to your local machine, and then just have a simple text file open in this window that can be open on both COSMOS and your local computer. This can then be a two-way clipboard between the two systems.
docs.title: Cut & Paste

docs.text: There are two main folders on COSMOS-SENS: After logging in you will land in your home folder ( /home/<userid> ). You will also have another folder called /scale/grXX/shared/ where all members of your group can put files to share. Files cannot be shared between groups, i.e, members of gr01 cannot send files to people in gr02. The two front-ends cannot touch.
docs.title: Where do I put my data?

docs.text: No Data on COSMOS-SENS does not have a backup. It is important you are comfortable in Linux environment, and so are individuals you add oto the project.
docs.title: Is my data backed up?

docs.text: Software at LUNARC is organised into modules which are loaded when needed, usually when a job is submitted. a rundown of the module system can be seen here , but lets load bowtie2 as an example: First we find the options available using module spider : $ module spider bowtie2 ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- Bowtie2: ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- Description: Bowtie 2 is an ultrafast and memory-efficient tool for aligning sequencing reads to long reference sequences. It is particularly good at aligning reads of about 50 up to 100s or 1,000s of characters, and particularly good at aligning to relatively long (e.g. mammalian) genomes. Bowtie 2 indexes the genome with an FM Index to keep its memory footprint small: for the human genome, its memory footprint is typically around 3.2 GB. Bowtie 2 supports gapped, local, and paired-end alignment modes. Versions: Bowtie2/2.2.6 Bowtie2/2.2.8 Bowtie2/2.2.9 Bowtie2/2.3.2 Bowtie2/2.3.4.1 Bowtie2/2.3.4.2 Bowtie2/2.4.4 ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- For detailed information about a specific "Bowtie2" module (including how to load the modules) use the module's full name. For example: $ module spider Bowtie2/2.3.4.1 ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- You can see there are several version available. To see how to load version 2.4.4 we need to run `module spider again: $ module spider Bowtie2/2.4.4 ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- Bowtie2: Bowtie2/2.4.4 ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- Description: Bowtie 2 is an ultrafast and memory-efficient tool for aligning sequencing reads to long reference sequences. It is particularly good at aligning reads of about 50 up to 100s or 1,000s of characters, and particularly good at aligning to relatively long (e.g. mammalian) genomes. Bowtie 2 indexes the genome with an FM Index to keep its memory footprint small: for the human genome, its memory footprint is typically around 3.2 GB. Bowtie 2 supports gapped, local, and paired-end alignment modes. You will need to load all module(s) on any one of the lines below before the "Bowtie2/2.4.4" module is available to load. GCC/10.3.0 So to load bowtie2, we also need to load the GCC/10.3.0 module. So we can now load bowtie2 by doing: $ module load GCC/10.3.0 Bowtie2/2.4.4 A short way of doing this is: $ ml GCC/10.3.0 Bowtie2/2.4.4 Done. If you have too many module conflicts happening, you can wipe the slate clean with: $ module purge
docs.title: Modules

docs.text: For software installation requests, raise a support ticket with LUNARC providing a link to the software that needs to be installed.
docs.title: Installing software

docs.text: When you login into COSMOS-SENS you will be located on the front-end (FE). THE FE is not a place to run long computations , only small interactive jobs. Long memory and processor intensive jobs must be sent to a compute node.
docs.title: Running jobs

docs.text: Any jobs such as making and mapping fastq files should be sent to the blades, and for this, LUNARC uses the SLURM job submission system. See below and here for basic guidelines on how to submit a job.
docs.title: SLURM

docs.text: Your project will have a project ID associated with it (csens20XX-X-X format). You need this to run a job. Lets say you want to map reads using bowtie, an example header for a job Run_bowtie.sh could look like this: #! /bin/bash #SBATCH -n 5 #SBATCH -N 1 #SBATCH -t 24:00:00 #SBATCH -A csens20XX-X-X #SBATCH -J BT2 #SBATCH -o BT2.%j.out #SBATCH -e BT2SingSing.%j.err module purge module load GCC/10.3.0 Bowtie2/2.4.4 bowtie2 <rest of the command here> In short -n 5 requests 5 CPU cores, -N 1 requests one node (do not ask for more), -t 24:00:00 kills the job after 24 hours, -A csens2024-3-2 specifies the project code, -J BT2 is the name of your job, -o BT2.%j.out is the outfile of the job (name+job id), -e BT2.%j.err is where the error log goes. The script is then run using: $ sbatch Run_bowtie.sh You can see your own jobs lining up using: $ sacct All jobs using: $ squeue If you know you have screwed something up and you want to kill a job: $ scancel <jobid>
docs.title: Project code

docs.text: If your program can use GPUs then you can run on the GPU nodes. You will need to add a partition parameter in your SLURM script so: #SBATCH -p sens-gpu Do not forget to load the CUDA modules if you need them: module load CUDA/12.1.1 There are fewer GPU nodes so the queue can be long for these.
docs.title: GPU nodes

docs.text: Most jobs create temporary files when running, so it makes sense (where possible) to use the local disk on each compute node to improve speed and reduce network traffic between the node and the storage. SLURM is set up to give you a temporary folder on the nodes for each job you start. The name of your temporary folder is stored in the $SNIC_TMP variable. This variable does not exist on the frontend, and the folder on the node is private to you and will be deleted once the job is finished. So in the last step of your script you need to save your results. For example, your script could look something like: STAR ...\\ --readFilesIn /somewhere/clusterPipeline/merged_cluster/*.gz \\ ... <rest of STAR command>\\ --outFileNamePrefix $SNIC_TMP/out/MyAnalysis_ cp $SNIC_TMP/out/MyAnalysis_* /home/<userid>/pathtofinaldestination/ So in this case, the output is directed to the local disk at $SNIC_TMP/out/MyAnalysis_ , and once mapping is complete the results are copied from there to your main storage in home .
docs.title: Run jobs using the local disk!

docs.text: Compute resources are sometimes limited, therefore try to use only the resources as you actually need for your jobs. Make sure you read the documents of the software you are using, and whether it can actually handle multi-core processes. There is no point in asking for 10 cores if your software cannot handle it.
docs.title: Be nice to fellow co-workers

docs.text: Never update packages in the middle of a project! . There is always a chance underlying methods change that may cause a change in the results. The best thing you can do is "freeze" your packages buy putting everything into a Apptainer (new name for Singularity) container/environment that you can use knowing that all package version are the same. Apptainer containers are also great for getting software onto COSMOS-SENS without needing LUNARC support to do an install. You can read more about Apptainer images here . Apptainer is installed on COSMOS-SENS and no modules are needed to load it. Apptainer images are very useful for packaging together workflows that require several programs to run one after another. Post-publication, these images can be included in the supporting material of your paper so others in your community can download it and apply it on their own data.
docs.title: Reproducible research

docs.text: The majority of users on COSMOS-SENS are bioinformaticians processing human sequence data. There are tools that people would like to use in a secure setting, so we will go through a few here.
docs.title: COSMOS-SENS and bioinformatics

docs.text: Note: this document has been updated to show how to run pipelines using Nexflow v24 . The previous document gave instructions for v23. Nextflow and the nf-core pipelines are a fantastic resource for bioinformaticians. There are a multitude of workflows for various NGS applications which go into real depth regarding QC, mapping methods, annotation, and reporting. After a pipeline is run, you also get the version numbers of the software used for easy reporting in papers, but importantly, the pipeline remains the same every time you run it ensuring results are comparable. When an nf-core pipeline is initiated, singularity images are pulled at runtime over the internet for each component program. As COSMOS-SENS is a secure server with no internet connection, pipelines and images have to be downloaded and then transferred to COSMOS-SENS beforehand.
docs.title: nf-core

docs.text: Read the nf-core docs, but to download a pipeline you need to install nf-core and then use nf-core tools download to begin the process of downloading a pipeline. You will need to download the singularity images when the option comes up. To make the pipelines available for all your project members, a good place to put them would be the shared area, for example /scale/grXX/shared/nf-core/ . When you download pipelines, make a folder called singularity_cache where the images are downloaded to. Use "copy" when the choice of "copy/amend" comes up during download process.
docs.title: Getting an nf-core pipeline

docs.text: To use them, you need to add a few lines into a file called .bash_profile which is in your home folder. 1) Open the file using gedit ~/.bash_profile 2) Add these lines at the end, and then save the file: export NXF_OFFLINE='true' export SINGULARITY_TMPDIR=$SNIC_TMP export NXF_SINGULARITY_LIBRARYDIR=/scale/grXX/shared/nf-core/singularity_cache export NXF_SINGULARITY_CACHEDIR="$NXF_SINGULARITY_LIBRARYDIR" export SINGULARITY_CACHEDIR="$NXF_SINGULARITY_LIBRARYDIR" export NXF_HOME=/scale/grXX/shared/nf-core/nextflow_sub/ export NXF_SINGULARITY_HOME_MOUNT=true Make sure you change the paths/name according to your project. You should then logout of COSMOS-SENS and log back in so these changes take effect . These lines set the environment variables that 1) Tells Nextflow where the singularity images are located ( /scale/gr01/shared/nf-core/singularity_cache ) 2) Set the temp dir to the ones located on the nodes ( $SNIC_TMP ). 3) Binds the singularity images to /scale so they can be found system wide. 4) Sets the home of Nextflow to the central copy on shared ( /scale/grXX/shared/nf-core/nextflow_sub/ ). This means each user doesn't need their own. When running a job, use the config file located here: /scale/gr01/shared/nf-core/cosmo_sens_grp1_NFv24.config This file contains the project ID and automatically sets the RAM and core resources so you don't have to.
docs.title: Setting up to use nf-core

docs.text: A sample sheet ( samplesheet.csv ) would look something like: sample,fastq_1,fastq_2,strandedness Sample1,Sample1_R1.fastq.gz,Sample1_R2.fastq.gz,auto Sample2,Sample2_R1.fastq.gz,Sample2_R2.fastq.gz,auto Sample3,Sample3_R1.fastq.gz,Sample3_R2.fastq.gz,auto and a script NFC_RNAseq.sh running the basic rnaseq pipline would look like this: module load Nextflow/24.10.0 nextflow run /scale/grXX/shared/nf-core/nf-core-rnaseq_3.17.0/3_17_0/main.nf \ -profile singularity \ --input samplesheet.csv \ -c /scale/grXX/shared/nf-core/cosmos_sens_grp1_NFv24.config \ --genome GRCm38 \ --igenomes_base /scale/references/AWS-iGenomes/ \ --outdir /home/<userid>/RNAseq_project/NFC_out This script, the fastq files, and the samplesheet are all in the same folder. The pipline is launched using: sh NFC_RNAseq.sh
docs.title: An example using RNAseq

docs.text: module load Nextflow/24.10.0 nextflow run /scale/gr01/shared/nf-core/nf-core-cutandrun_3.2.2/3_2_2/main.nf \ --input samplesheet.csv \ -profile singularity \ -c /scale/gr01/shared/nf-core/cosmos_sens_grp1_NFv24.config \ --fasta /scale/references/AWS-iGenomes/Homo_sapiens/Ensembl/GRCh37/Sequence/WholeGenomeFasta/genome.fa \ --gtf /scale/references/AWS-iGenomes/Homo_sapiens/Ensembl/GRCh37/Annotation/Genes \ --spikein_bowtie2 /scale/references/AWS-iGenomes/Escherichia_coli_K_12_MG1655/NCBI/2001-10-15/Sequence/Bowtie2Index \ --spikein_fasta /scale/references/AWS-iGenomes/Escherichia_coli_K_12_MG1655/NCBI/2001-10-15/Sequence/WholeGenomeFasta/genome.fa \ --outdir /home/<userid>/<path_to_out>/CaR_Out
docs.title: Cut&Run

docs.text: The contents of the sample sheet will vary depending on which pipline you are using, so be sure to read the manual.
docs.title: Sample sheets

docs.text: nf-core pipelines will make a work folder if the tmp folder on the node isn't used. Delete this folder when you are done! It is normally huge and contains nothing of interest.
docs.title: Remove the work folder

docs.text: The available pipelines are located in /scale/gr01/shared/nf-core . If the one you need is missing, contact Petter for it to be downloaded.
docs.title: Available pipelines

docs.text: Some well-based methods generate thousands of small fastq files which do not play nice with the queuing system on CSENS when using an nf-core pipeline. The jobs are fired-off to the nodes so quickly that SLURM cannot keep up, but importantly, setting up the task actually takes longer than the compute subsequently done. If you are in this situation, you need to run the pipeline locally on a single node instead. This means all the pipeline steps will be carried out on single server, and not distributed over multiple nodes which is what normally happens. Do this this you have to used a different config file, namely cosmos_sens_grp1_NFv24_local.config . So, to use RNAseq as an example you would submit a job like so: #! /bin/bash #SBATCH -n 48 #SBATCH -N 1 #SBATCH -t 24:00:00 #SBATCH -A csens2024-3-2 #SBATCH -J nfc_rnaseq #SBATCH -o nfc_rnaseq.%j.out #SBATCH -e nfc_rnaseq.%j.err module load Nextflow/24.10.0 nextflow run /scale/gr01/shared/nf-core/nf-core-rnaseq_3.17.0/3_17_0/main.nf \ -profile singularity \ --input samplesheet.csv \ -c /scale/gr01/shared/nf-core/cosmos_sens_grp1_NFv24_local.config \ --genome GRCm38 \ --igenomes_base /references/AWS-iGenomes/ \ --outdir /home/<userid>/RNAseq_project/NFC_out This will run the entire pipeline on a single node.
docs.title: If you have many small fastq files

docs.text: Software can be packaged into Apptainer containers that provide a complete analysis environment that can be copied over to COSMOS-SENS and be used there. This means you get exactly what you need, and also reduces the workload on the good people at LUNARC. This is also an excellent way of practicing reproducible research . A project can be done using an immutable Apptainer image, so if you need to go back to the project in X years time, you have the original software setup you had when you first did it. If you upgrade a piece of software in your image, you can make a new version of it so the previous version still exists in the original state. It's easier to make an image on a Linux system if you are going to use it on COSMOS-SENS. If you use a Mac, your best bet is to use open COSMOS to make the image which you can copy to COSMOS-SENS. We have a tutorial which Stefan Lang has written showing how to make images on COSMOS that you can read here . If you are making an image on your own Linux machine , an example is given below.
docs.title: Apptainer (Singularity) containers

docs.text: This is an Apptainer definition file for creating a container based on Alpine Linux with Python, JupyterLab, R, and R-Jupyter integration. We use Alpine Linux for this because it produces slim images that take up less space. Put the following into a file called Apptainer_example.def : Bootstrap: docker From: alpine:latest # Use the latest Alpine Linux image as the base %post # Update the package index and install essential packages apk update # Install build tools and libraries required for Python and R # You must not have comments after the '\' in the following lines! apk add --no-cache bash \ build-base \ zeromq-dev \ libffi-dev \ musl-dev \ openblas-dev \ R \ R-dev \ R-doc \ python3 \ py3-pip \ python3-dev \ py3-setuptools \ py3-wheel # Allow pip to modify system-wide packages (ChatGPT forgets that ALWAYS) export PIP_BREAK_SYSTEM_PACKAGES=1 # Install JupyterLab using pip pip3 install --no-cache-dir jupyterlab # Install R packages for Jupyter integration R -e "install.packages(c('IRkernel', 'IRdisplay'), repos='https://cloud.r-project.org/')" # Set up IRkernel to make R available as a Jupyter kernel R -e "IRkernel::installspec(user = FALSE)" %environment # Ensure /usr/local/bin is in the PATH so JupyterLab can be found export PATH="/usr/local/bin:$PATH" # if you want to install more python packages in the sandbox: export PIP_BREAK_SYSTEM_PACKAGES=1 %runscript # By default, run JupyterLab when the container starts jupyter lab --port 9734 --ip=0.0.0.0 --allow-root --no-browser To build a sandbox for manual modification, run this command: apptainer build --sandbox Apptainer_example Apptainer_example.def Shell into the sandbox: apptainer shell --writable Apptainer_example From here you can now install anything else you might need using Alpine's apk add --no-cache command. After you have installed everything, including the jupyter lab server, you can test it with: apptainer run Apptainer_example If you're happy, you can then go ahead and build the image: apptainer build Apptainer_example.sif Apptainer_example The image can now be copied to COSMOS-SENS and used there using: apptainer run Apptainer_example.sif Again, if you are making an image on COSMOS you need to read Stefan's tutorial .
docs.title: Minimal example (taken from Stefan's tutorial).
